QF.id: XIII Introduction to the Underlying Markets_16

question.text: What distinguishes equity securities from debt securities as investment instruments?

answer.text: Equity represents ownership in a company with variable returns; debt represents a loan to the issuer with fixed or determinable returns
Equity always pays regular dividends; debt never pays any periodic income
Equity has a fixed maturity date; debt has no maturity and is perpetual
Equity is only traded on exchanges; debt is only traded over-the-counter

explanation.text: The Logic: NISM Series IV pages 68-69 explain that financing happens through borrow-lend of cash in the money and bond markets and through buy-sell of business ownership in equity markets. Debt is described as borrowed money repaid with interest; equity is described as raising money by selling a stake in the business — hence the ownership-versus-loan and variable-versus-fixed-return distinction. The Trap: Equity dividends are not guaranteed and can be skipped, so "always pays dividends" is wrong. Equity typically has no fixed maturity while debt does, so the maturity statement is reversed. Both equity and debt instruments can trade on exchanges and OTC, so that distinction is also incorrect. Note: Residual-claim wording, trading-venue comparisons and derivative-pricing implications are not covered in the pages checked and are intentionally not used in this explanation.
